name: Sevoflurane
route_note: Inhaled via a calibrated vaporiser in oxygen with or without nitrous oxide or air.
originator: Travenol Laboratories (Ross Terrell, Bernard Regan); developed by Maruishi (Japan)

discovery.note: Synthesised in the late 1960s–early 1970s among fluorinated ethers; development stalled in the US until Maruishi took it forward in Japan.

tagline: Sweet-smelling volatile anaesthetic ideal for gas induction in children
summary: Sevoflurane is a fluorinated ether volatile anaesthetic used for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia. Because it is non-pungent and has low blood solubility, it allows smooth, rapid inhalational induction, particularly in children, and fast emergence.
mechanism: Like other volatile anaesthetics, sevoflurane enhances inhibitory GABA-A and glycine receptor function, activates two-pore-domain potassium channels and inhibits excitatory NMDA and nicotinic receptors. Immobility is mediated mainly at the spinal cord and unconsciousness at supraspinal networks.
Its low blood:gas partition coefficient (about 0.65) means alveolar and brain concentrations change quickly, giving rapid onset and offset. The minimum alveolar concentration in adults is about 2%.
uses: Induction of general anaesthesia (especially inhalational induction in children)
Maintenance of general anaesthesia in adults and children

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Sevoflurane is synthesised among fluorinated ethers at Travenol Laboratories.

history.title: First report
history.detail: Wallin and colleagues publish its anaesthetic properties.

history.title: Japan
history.detail: Maruishi gains approval in Japan, where it is widely used first.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Abbott's Ultane is approved in the US.

history.title: Compound A
history.detail: Studies examine nephrotoxic Compound A formed by reaction with carbon dioxide absorbents, leading to fresh gas flow recommendations.

history.title: Climate focus
history.detail: The EU's revised F-gas regulation restricts desflurane from 2026 because of its far higher global warming potential, favouring agents such as sevoflurane.

pk.half_life: Elimination mainly by exhalation; rapid washout (low blood:gas coefficient ~0.65)
pk.metabolism: About 2–5% hepatic CYP2E1 metabolism to hexafluoroisopropanol and inorganic fluoride

facts: Its low pungency makes it the standard agent for gas induction in children.
Sevoflurane's global warming potential is much lower than desflurane's.
